docs.title: Erazure's PD2 Loot Filter
docs.text: A highly stylized loot filter for Project Diablo 2, with multiple filter level tiers for customizable strictness and colorful, intuitive symbols for runes, gems, maps, charms and more.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
1. In the PD2 launcher, open Item Filter Profiles, pick Erazure - Main and click Save Filter on the right side. Not sure which version? Main is the one to start with; Versions says what the others change.
  2. In game, pick your filter level: Esc > Options > PD2 Options, or the Increase / Decrease Filter Level hotkeys (set them in Configure Controls). Your Horadric Cube's description shows the version and level you're on.
  3. Start on level 1, Lowest Strictness: it's for the ladder start and characters up to level ~80. Move to a stricter level as your character outgrows its drops; Filter Levels shows what each one hides.

The launcher keeps the filter up to date: each update reaches you the next time you press Play. The filter is updated for the Season 14 Alliance ladder; last updated November 20th, 2026 (what's new).

  • Each row is one case: the filter levels it applies to, what happens, and what the item needs. Every column must hold; any means no condition. Pick your filter level in the bar to see only your rows.
  • ED is enhanced defense on armor and enhanced damage on weapons (superior items). Class items roll +1–3 to skills; a runeword base with several skill combinations opens to list them.
  • Bases of one type and tier with the same socket maximum, size and rows share a group.
  • Ethereal weapons with no sockets that a class would corrupt into a rare (bricking) get a red star and a note while you play that class: the Class column names it.
  • Hidden items still show in town. The minimap icon and chat notification come on their own, even for a hidden item. Low quality items (Cracked, Crude, Damaged) have their own rows when they differ.

docs.title: Edit by Hand
docs.text:
The easiest way to change Erazure is the Filter Editor: it builds your own copy in your browser (looks, sounds, items, your own rules) and saves it straight into your game, and your changes carry over to every Erazure update. This page is for editing a copy of the filter file by hand.

A hand-edited copy doesn't update

The launcher's Erazure updates by itself; your own copy stays on the day you downloaded it. After each Erazure update, download the new file and make your edits again. Already have a hand-edited copy and tired of that? Paste the rules you wrote into the Filter Editor's My rules: it adds them to every new Erazure for you.

docs.title: Edit a copy
docs.text:
1. In the launcher, open Item Filter Profiles, pick Erazure and the version you want, and click Copy to Local: it copies that version into Diablo II\ProjectD2\filters\local. (Or download the file from the filter's GitHub page, such as Erazure-Main.filter, and save it in that folder.)
  2. Open the file in your text editor (VS Code or Notepad++), make your edits and save it, as a .filter file.
  3. In the launcher, open Item Filter Profiles, click Local Filter, pick your file and click Save Filter.
  4. In game, press the reload filter key (Numpad 0 unless you changed it in Configure Controls), or start the game.

The file is about 2.4 MB, and some lines are very long: the filter's shorthand (its aliases) is written out in every rule, which makes the game load it faster. The Filter Editor shows Erazure's rules in their short form (Erazure's rules), and its My rules checks each rule you write as the game reads it.

docs.title: Tags and highlights
docs.text:
Once an item is identified, the line under its name holds the filter's tags: its best stats in short, 30fcr, 45r, 3mpk. A unique's or set item's tags are its rolls. A line between stars is a highlight (Skill & Shop Highlights lists them all), and notes such as Max Sockets and Upgrade, with its recipe, come under the name too. Screenshots from the game:

A rare ring: damage, dexterity, two resistances and mana after each kill, and the Physical highlight.

Rare boots: run speed, life and three resistances, their upgrade and the recipe for it, and the Triple Resist highlight.

Rare gloves: cast rate, curse duration, enhanced defense and maximum mana.

A magic small charm: maximum damage, attack rating and life, and the Physical highlight.

A rare ethereal sword: its sockets after the name, attack speed, enhanced damage and damage to undead, its runes, and the Enhanced Damage highlight.

A mirrored rare maul: enhanced damage and crushing blow, six sockets of runes, and the Enhanced Damage highlight.

The Stone of Jordan: its rolls (mana, maximum mana) and its corruption's damage reduction, with a highlight.

Death's Web: its poison and bone skills, enemy poison resistance roll, and the corruption's cast rate and fire skill damage.

Guardian Angel: skills and maximum resistances, how many sockets it can still get (L: Larzuk, P: Puzzlebox, C: corruption), and its upgrade with the recipe for it.

Tal Rasha's Guardianship: its magic damage reduction and magic find rolls.

Magic gloves in a shop: their sell value, +3 to Javelin and Spear Skills with 20% attack speed, and the +3/20ias highlight.

docs.title: Maps
docs.text:
An identified map's hover box opens with its tags (experience, monster rarity, monster density, magic find), then its area level, the highest resistances and the immunities of its monsters, its guest monsters and its mods to watch out for: gray for a small roll, red for a dangerous one. A high monster rarity or density roll stands between stars, more of them the higher it is. Under them come its experience lines: on an uncorrupted map the tag, 1.80x Experience, is how much more a full clear gives with the map's rolls than without them (is it worth corrupting?), and on every map 2.10x at Level 90 is what it gives you at your level against the average plain T1-T3 map, for the same distance walked. Map Experience explains both. These pictures are from before November 17th, when both numbers had one decimal, corrupted maps showed the tag too and the lines came in another order.

A rare T1 map: two small rolls in gray, crushing blow in red, +40% Monster Rarity between stars, 1.6x Experience and 1.8x at level 90.

A rare T2 map with Fetishes as guest monsters, two kinds of extra elemental damage and less chance to block in red, +84% Monster Density between stars, 1.5x Experience and 1.9x at level 90.

A corrupted rare T3 map: all four tags, +62% Monster Rarity between stars, 1.8x Experience and 2.1x at level 90. Corrupted, it shows no area level, highest resistances or small rolls.

docs.title: Filter Levels
docs.text:
Pick your filter level in game: Esc > Options > PD2 Options, or with the Increase / Decrease Filter Level hotkeys (set them in Configure Controls). The Horadric Cube's description says which level you are on.

Super Healing and Super Mana Potions show on every filter level. To hide healing or mana potions on any level, turn on Hide Healing Potions or Hide Mana Potions in the game's Loot Filter options: they hide every healing or mana potion, whatever the filter level.

How to read it

What each filter level of the Erazure loot filter shows, notifies and hides, for every kind of item that drops, read from the filter's own rules: the table first, then what changes from one level to the next. Pick your level in game (Esc > Options > PD2 Options, or the Increase / Decrease Filter Level hotkeys); the Horadric Cube's description says which level you are on.

  • Shown for Erazure - Main, on the ground outside town in Nightmare and Hell; a cell's details add what Normal difficulty and special areas change.
  • Each column is a group of filter levels that behave the same; levels that differ only in the Rejuvenation Potion (35%) share one (3-4, 5-6).
  • Many items hide only once your character reaches a level: from clvl 80 means from character level 80. The strip under a cell shows character levels 1 to 99, hatched where items hide. Type your character level in the bar to see your own.
  • Click a cell for its details: which items, when, and what changes in Normal difficulty and special areas. The rows link to the pages with every base and item.
  • Hidden items still show in town, and unique and set items still show until you've discovered them (Discovery Progress). Level 0 hides nothing.
  • Unique and set items drop unidentified: one row per value tier. Non-magical items: two rows each, plain (no sockets, not superior, no skills) and best case (the most a base can show with any sockets, enhanced defense or damage, or skills); the Non-magical Bases page has every base.

What the box reads and what each button does
  • Quickest: open the Compendium view and page through it beside the game's own Compendium, clicking the cards you've discovered.
  • Found most of it? Type what you're missing in the box, one name per line, and press "Mark all but these discovered": every other item is marked discovered. In game, the stash's Uniques and Sets tabs list what you're missing when you turn on "Show Undiscovered" (hover an item for its name). Or press "Mark all discovered" and mark the missing ones undiscovered one by one under Every Item: type a name in its search and press Enter.
  • Found a few? Type them in the box and press "Mark these discovered", or click their boxes under Every Item. For a whole set or base at once, search it there and press "Mark listed items discovered".
  • The box's buttons: "Mark these discovered" adds the names to your list, "Mark these undiscovered" takes them off, "Mark all but these discovered" marks every item discovered but the names, and "Replace my list" marks the names discovered and everything else undiscovered.
  • What the box reads: one item per line, from a spreadsheet, another grail tracker or typed by hand (Harlequin Crest, Arm of King Leoric). Capitals, apostrophes, a leading "The", bullets, numbering and a checked box such as [x] don't matter, a version in brackets counts as the item (Harlequin Crest (Shako)), and a spreadsheet row counts by the cell with the name. Lines with an empty box ([ ], ✗) and rows marked no, false, 0 or ✗ are skipped, and the lines it doesn't recognize are listed under the buttons (the first 10). Items that don't count for the grail (How It's Worked Out names them) are listed apart.
  • Keep or move your list: "Copy" copies the list of your discovered items ("Show my list" shows it in the box). On another browser or device, paste it into this box and press "Replace my list".
  • Undo takes back your changes one at a time, latest first, while you stay on the page.

docs.title: How It's Worked Out
docs.text:
• The grail: every unique and set item in the game, unique maps, quest items and nine uniques that don't count for the grail left out (Itherael's Path, Overlord's Helm, Dark Abyss, Aidan's Scar, Hadriel's Hand, Band of Skulls, Cage of the Unsullied, The Third Eye and Rainbow Facet). An item that comes in several versions (Akarat's Devotion, Cyclopean Roar and Arm of King Leoric, two versions each) is one grail item: any of its versions finds it, so its chances are those of all its versions together.
  • Drops: each monster's drops and their quality as the game rolls them: each base's chance to be unique or set at the monster's level (class items have their own, better chances), magic find with its diminishing returns, and a unique picked among the base's uniques by their weight. A unique roll on a base with no unique becomes a rare, a set roll with no set item magic.
  • Maps: full clears, averaged over the maps of a tier, from the map model behind the filter's experience tags (monsters per area, elite packs, monster levels; the website's Map Experience page explains it). "Rare" is the average rare map with a corruption: its density, monster rarity and magic find. Solo; one map boss per map, each map's own: its own loot at its own level (80 to 91; map bosses keep their level as other bosses do).
  • The Bitter Depths: the map event in about 1 rare T1-T3 map in 26 and 1 non-magical map in 82 (its portal always opens, late in the clear). Its 20 Lucion's chests drop as a tier-0 vault's do, 5 items each; its monsters (5 elite packs) and Zoltun Kulle drop as map monsters do, and your ear works on them, not on the chests. The map's magic find carries into it, for the chests too. Zoltun's death also sets off a treasure explosion: his loot again and again until 60 items lie on the ground, at his level, with no magic find (your ear doesn't touch it either). Its 7 sparkly chests are left out (about 3% of its chests' grail drops). Every map's numbers include it at that chance.
  • Cow King's Leathers: only a Hell Bovine's drop can be one of its pieces: the cows of the Secret Cow Level and the Cow King. Blood Moon's cows are other monsters and never drop it. Maps have Hell Bovines two ways, and the page counts both for these three items: the Bovine guest ("Map contains Hell Bovines"), a prefix on about 1 rare T1 map in 18 and 1 rare T2 or T3 map in 28, which adds the cows to every area's monsters (in groups and elite packs, beside the map's own) with +25-30% density and +15-20% magic find; and the Dark Wanderer map event, whose three wanderers each turn into a random act boss or superunique: the Cow King, with his 8 Hell Bovines, in about 1 rare map in 260 and 1 non-magical map in 800 (an event always brings all three).
  • Grail progress: each item drops at random at its own rate, so the items found after n maps add up item by item. "Switching" works from the expected progress; with your real list the planner does better.
  • Farm spots: one kill of each act boss and superunique in each difficulty, solo: the monster's own drop at its own level. The drops of the minions around a superunique are counted apart, as "with its minions". In Normal difficulty a monster has a fixed level of its own; in Nightmare and Hell it takes the area's level, but bosses keep theirs; superuniques and their minions are 3 levels higher. A kill makes at most six items, gold and potions included, so Duriel's many drop rolls always end at six. A boss drops its quest loot only while the quest is open; farming kills drop the usual loot.
  • Spots: "fixed" means the monster stands in the same place every game: its area is one of the game's preset maps (the Cathedral, Tower Cellar Level 5, Nihlathak's Temple...), or laid out the same way every game (Travincal, the Chaos Sanctuary, the Bloody Foothills), or it waits in a piece the game always puts at the same edge of its area (Eldritch by the Bloody Foothills, Stormtree in the Flayer Jungle at its border with Lower Kurast). The others stand in a piece of the area the game places anywhere in it. "Areas from a waypoint" counts the areas to walk through from the nearest waypoint (towns have one; portals count as one step).
  • Corrupted Zones: in Hell games made with Baal's quest done, one group of areas at a time has area level 85, so its superuniques are level 88 (bosses keep their own level).
  • Ubers and events:
    • Lilith, Uber Duriel and Uber Izual drop their own loot at level 110.
    • Diablo Clone drops Annihilus every kill; Uber Tristram drops the Hellfire Torch once a run, when its last boss dies (the three bosses drop nothing else).
    • The Uber Ancients: before touching the altar you switch on the ancients you want to fight at their statues, one, two or all three; the altar then drops 20 to 29 items for one ancient, 32 to 47 for two and 44 to 65 for three, at item level 90.
    • Lucion's vault has 10 chests at every tier (0, 1 and 2, easiest first); each drops 3 items, then 2, 3 or 4 more from better loot on tier 0, 1 or 2, so a harder tier gives more items, not better ones. The items have the vault's level (89); the level of the character who opens the chest (95 here) goes into their quality. The numbers are for the whole vault; Lucion himself drops no grail items.
    • The vault's key is cubed from three parts, each a chance per kill in Hell (Lucion's Chests names them; solo, as every number here).
  • Unique map bosses: the bosses of four unique maps drop extra loot when they die, on top of their own. Unique maps open only in Hell, one a game; one run a map, and the rest of the map isn't counted.
    • Three drop random uniques: Gregus Mazi in City of Ureh 3 (socketed), Warlord of Blood 2 or 3 (corrupted) and Na-Krul in Na-Krul's Abyss 3 (ethereal, but for the indestructible ones).
    • Each starts as a unique picked at random, every unique alike but the few with no rarity (Embersworn among them; Rainbow Facets are in; Gregus Mazi passes over bases that take no sockets). Na-Krul drops the unique he picked.
    • Warlord of Blood and Gregus Mazi keep only its base and make a unique of it at item level 99, picked as any dropped unique is, by how common each unique of that base is (one already dropped in the game comes out rare).
    • Their own loot drops as a map boss's does, at their level (91), with the map's own magic find.
    • Djinn's Domain's two Djinns, Siren of the Forgotten Vault and Djinn of a Thousand Blades, each set off a treasure explosion when they die: their own loot again and again until 60 items lie on the ground, at their level (90), with no magic find. Their own loot drops too, twice (Djinn's Domain repeats every monster's drop) and a third time half the time (the map's extra drop).
    • The minibosses (Zayl the Merciful in City of Ureh, Cory the Imp and Onion the Accused in Warlord of Blood) drop only their own loot, as their map's boss does (level 91). A run counts it: players kill them too.
  • T4 dungeons: one run a dungeon, a whole clear of its two floors, the average of the three dungeons. The cube makes them rare: an average rare dungeon with a corruption (+148% density, +27% monster rarity, and +161% magic find on top of yours).
    • Every monster killed in a T4 dungeon drops its own loot twice, the bosses too; a unique monster's minions drop theirs once.
    • Its two bosses, one on its first floor and one on its last, each set off a treasure explosion when they die: the first floor's boss until 30 items lie on the ground, the last floor's until 60, at the boss's level (92; Skullsplitter Cyrus 90), with no magic find. Their loot, explosions and own alike, is the Uber Ancients' altar's. The three dungeons' bosses drop alike.
    • Dungeons are dangerous and deadly: every monster has several immunities, so few builds can clear one, and a dungeon can take upwards of 45 minutes to an hour or longer. The page weighs a dungeon against the full map clears 45 minutes to an hour holds (15 minutes each, the estimated time of Map Event and Boss Rushing).
  • Best bet: an item's best bet compares one kill with one map: target farming its best boss or superunique (any difficulty; Corrupted Zones, ubers, events, unique map bosses and T4 dungeon bosses left out) when one kill there finds it at least as often as a whole map with the item's best ear, maps otherwise. That's as if a kill took as long as a map; a quicker kill makes farming better still. Your Grail's plan sorts your missing items by it, and splits the maps' ones by their chance in your next 100 maps with the ear it names: an even chance or better, or the slowest.
  • Gheed's map event (its tab): each of his 5 offers is a random unique: any unique but jewels and the few with no rarity (Embersworn among them). One that needs character level 60 or more is turned down (level − 49)% of the time and another picked; in one shop in 200, one offer is a special ring instead.
  • Gambling: each gambled item's item level is your character level −5 to +4. The base becomes exceptional with a chance that grows 0.9% per item level above the exceptional version's level, else elite with 0.33% per level above the elite version's (only once the exceptional chance is above zero). Then it is unique 1 time in 2,000 and a set item 1 time in 1,000, picked among the uniques or sets of that base whose level is at most the item level, like a drop; with none, the roll is lost. Magic find plays no part. The gold: rings 50,000, amulets 63,000; any other base costs more the higher your character level, and the more so the higher its exceptional and elite versions' prices (no reduced vendor prices here). Cow King's Leathers never comes from gambling. Gambling ranks the bases.
  • Magic find: the bar is your character's magic find. Unique, set and rare chances grow with it, ever slower (the game's diminishing returns). A map's own magic find adds to yours before them, as the game does: ; the unique maps add their own.
  • Left out:
    • The rest of a unique map (only its bosses count).
    • The map events but the Bitter Depths (Treasure Fallen, Corrupted Heroes, Horazon, the Dark Wanderer and the rest; Gheed's shop has its own tab), and map guests. Cow King's Leathers alone counts the Bovine guest and the Dark Wanderer's Cow King. The website's Map Event and Boss Rushing page counts every event.
    • A rare map's extra weapon, armor and crafting drops (some of its suffixes).
    • Magic maps, Fortified maps and parties (the notes on the Corrupted Ears tab say what the last two change).
    • Whole area clears: a full Cow Level, Chaos Sanctuary or Baal run also drops from every monster on the way, so those runs find more than the boss alone shows here.
    • PD2's special drops (sigils, Corrupted Zone shards) aren't grail items.
Words on this page 1 in 1,200 mapsA chance, not a promise: on average one drop every 1,200 full map clears. A 90% chance to see the item takes about 2.3 times that many; luck runs ahead or behind. Kills, runs, maps, dungeons, vaults, shops, gamblesFarm spots count per kill; per run for Uber Tristram and the Uber Ancients (one, two or three ancients, your choice at their statues); per map for the unique map bosses (one run of the map); per dungeon for a T4 dungeon (a whole one, or its two bosses); per vault (its 10 chests) for Lucion's vault; per shop for Gheed's map event; per gamble (with its gold) for gambling; per run for the Bitter Depths (its chests, monsters and Zoltun Kulle), which every map's numbers count at the event's chance. A kill and a map clear take very different times, so compare spots with spots and maps with maps. No ear, Any ear, Best earAn item's chance per map without a Corrupted Ear, with an ear whose pool doesn't have the item's base (what every ear gives), and with the ear whose pool has it. Best ear ×How many times more often the best ear finds an item than no ear. Maps for 90%The maps for a 90% chance to see an item. Best betWhere an item comes from best: target farming its best boss or superunique when one kill there finds it at least as often as a whole map with its best ear ("beats maps"), maps otherwise. A kill = 3 mapsOne kill finds the item as often as 3 maps with its best ear: farming wins as long as a kill takes you less time than 3 maps. Drop levelThe lowest monster level that can drop an item: not the level you need to wear it. The farm spots reach level 68 in Normal and 75 in Nightmare, so the highest-level items only come from Hell. Normal, Nightmare, HellThe difficulties. A "normal base" (beside exceptional and elite) is an item's base tier. Fixed spot, random spotA fixed spot is the same every game (the Cathedral, Travincal, Nihlathak's Temple); a random one is anywhere in its area. Areas from a waypointThe areas to walk through from the nearest waypoint (towns have one; a portal counts as one step). With its minionsA superunique's own drop is the main number; "with its minions" adds the monsters around it. Corrupted ZoneIn Hell games made with Baal's quest done, one group of areas at a time has area level 85, so its superuniques drop at level 88 while the zone lasts. Ubers and eventsLilith, Uber Duriel, Uber Izual, Diablo Clone, Uber Tristram, the Uber Ancients and Lucion's vault. A modelThe numbers follow how the game rolls drops (what each monster can drop, its quality, magic find) and the map model behind the filter's experience tags, solo: estimates, not a drop log.

How the Erazure loot filter shows magic items that drop on the ground, unidentified, read from the filter's own rules. At the filter levels a base's rows don't cover, it shows with its plain name in blue, with Eth before it when it is ethereal.

Notify minimap icon and chat notification, and a drop sound where one is shown Shows as a look of its own (shown as the game draws it) Hidden the item is not shown
  • Each row is one case: the filter levels it applies to, what happens, and what the item needs. Every column must hold; any means no condition. Pick your filter level in the bar to see only your rows.
  • Crafted affix level is the affix level the filter works out for a craft made from the item: from half your character level plus half its item level.
  • Bases of one type and tier with the same socket maximum and rows share a group. A look shows the group's first base; each base shows its own name.
  • Hidden items still show in town. The minimap icon and chat notification come on their own, even for a hidden item.
  • Charms drop only as magic items (the game has no rare charms). The number after the dot in a charm's look is its item level; a row shows its lowest.

How the Erazure loot filter shows rare items that drop on the ground, unidentified, read from the filter's own rules. At the filter levels a base's rows don't cover, it shows with its plain name in yellow, with Eth before it when it is ethereal.

Notify minimap icon and chat notification, and a drop sound where one is shown Shows as a look of its own (shown as the game draws it) Hidden the item is not shown
  • Each row is one case: the filter levels it applies to, what happens, and what the item needs. Every column must hold; any means no condition. Pick your filter level in the bar to see only your rows.
  • Crafted affix level is the affix level the filter works out for a craft made from the item: from half your character level plus half its item level.
  • Bases of one type and tier with the same socket maximum and rows share a group. A look shows the group's first base; each base shows its own name.
  • Hidden items still show in town. The minimap icon and chat notification come on their own, even for a hidden item.
  • The PoE versions of the filter play their own drop sound for rare jewels.

How the Erazure loot filter shows unique and set items that drop unidentified: the tier each one is in, and when the others are shown quietly or hidden. Everything here is read from the filter's own rules. Once identified, an item shows its stats instead.

  • Each line is one case: when it applies, the tier, the label as the game draws it, the minimap icon and the drop sound. A tier named alone notifies as usual (see Tiers); otherwise the difference follows in brackets.
  • Press ▶ beside a sound to hear it. Point at the sound for its number: type .playsound and that number in game to hear it there.
  • Items on the same base share a tier. Unidentified, the filter cannot tell them apart: Lightsabre and Azurewrath are both a Phase Blade.
  • Hidden items still show their name in town. Until you've discovered an item (the Holy Grail Discovery Progress) it is never hidden and always gets a minimap icon and a chat notification when it drops, on every filter level, and a drop sound (its own, or the Grail sound where it has none), and wherever it isn't High or Medium value (set rings and amulets too) it shows the Grail look: an orange star on each side (a Minimal value unique and a Medium value set item have a Grail look of their own). An item on a base with several uniques, like Thunder Maul, counts as discovered once you've found all of them.
  • The game's Force Show Unowned option (in its Loot Filter options, off by default) also shows the ones you have discovered but don't own yet where the filter would hide them, with the game's plain name instead of these looks.

docs.title: Versions of the Filter
docs.text: Not sure? Pick Erazure - Main. Every other version is Main with a different look, or with one or more of three changes added.

docs.title: Pick one in the launcher
docs.text:
1. In the PD2 launcher, open Item Filter Profiles and pick Erazure in the list of authors.
  2. Click a version, then Save Filter on the right side.
  3. In game, hover your Horadric Cube: its description names the version, your filter level and the date of the update you have. Pick your filter level in game too (Filter Levels says how).

The launcher keeps the filter up to date: each update reaches you the next time you press Play, with no need to save again.

docs.title: What the versions change
docs.text:
A version is a look plus any of three changes; every combination is in the launcher.

Look Erazure The colorful symbols around item names (see them in game). Minimal The same filter with fewer, simpler symbols (every label that differs). Corrlorized Corr's restyle: his own colors, symbols and Path of Exile sound picks, with the same filter levels. Only with PoE. Add What it changes Revealed Unidentified unique and set items show their identified names when they drop. BIG GG - Mystery The best drops hide what they are on the ground, outside town: BIG GG for Sur, Ber, Jah, Cham, Zod, Vial of Lightsong, Lilith's Mirror, Horadric Almanac and the Diablo Clone and Rathma uniques; LIL GG for Vex, Ohm, Lo, Larzuk's Puzzlebox, Horadric Navigator, Demonic Cube and Skeleton Key. You find out when you pick it up. PoE Path of Exile sound effects on valuable drops.

docs.title: How it’s worked out
docs.text:
• The weapon: an ethereal weapon has 5/4 of its base damage, rounded down. Enhanced damage on the weapon (its own, a superior base’s, its sockets’) raises only the base damage: base + base × enhanced damage / 100, rounded down; then its flat minimum and maximum damage are added.
  • The attack: the weapon’s damage plus flat damage from other gear, times (100 + the attack skill’s damage + your auras’ and buffs’ damage + Strength × the weapon’s Strength bonus / 100 + Dexterity × its Dexterity bonus / 100 + your weapon mastery + damage against demons or undead when the monster is one + enhanced damage from other gear) / 100; a melee hit with a blunt weapon (a mace, hammer, club, scepter, wand or staff) adds 50 more against undead, an arrow or a thrown weapon doesn’t. Your character screen leaves the part against demons or undead out. A minimum below 1 becomes 1 and a maximum at or below the minimum becomes the minimum + 1, before the percentages. The game keeps it in 256ths of a point; a hit is any damage from the minimum to the maximum alike. A skill that deals part of the weapon’s damage (Stun, Guided Arrow, Blade Fury) takes that part.
  • Your own aura gives you its full damage bonus; a party member’s or your mercenary’s gives half (the “Party Damage” of the tooltip).
  • Critical strike comes first: chance (Amazon’s Critical Strike, items, a mastery) at most 75%, double damage plus the critical strike multiplier. Only a hit that isn’t critical can be a deadly strike: chance at most 75% plus maximum deadly strike, 1.5 times damage plus the deadly strike multiplier.
  • Physical resistance: the monster’s resistance plus a curse, Amplify Damage or Decrepify (Weaken and Attract leave it), and Battle Cry, which is no curse and goes with any. A monster holds one curse and one Battle Cry at a time, so what a build puts on it itself (Curses and debuffs on its card: its own skill, charges, a chance to cast on striking, Call to Arms’ Battle Cry) replaces the party’s (the monster’s fields), which every other build keeps. Against a monster whose own resistance is 100% or more, curses and Battle Cry count half. Physical pierce lowers what is left below 100%, and below 0% it counts half. Damage is lowered by the resistance (raised at negative resistance, at most double).
  • Chance to hit: every hit rolls on its own, and only a hit that lands does damage or a crushing blow. Attack rating = (5 × Dexterity − 35 + the class’s own (Amazon and Druid 5, Assassin 15, Barbarian and Paladin 20, Necromancer −10, Sorceress −15) + attack rating on gear and from Grim Ward, + attack rating against demons or undead when the monster is one) × (100 + attack rating % on gear + from your auras and buffs (Fanaticism, Concentration, Blessed Aim, Heart of Wolverine, your own Holy aura, a wereform’s by Lycanthropy’s level, Penetrate’s level) + the attack skill’s own + your weapon mastery’s on a melee hit) / 100, rounded down. Your character screen shows it with the attack on a mouse button, without the part against demons or undead; with a throw skill and a throwing weapon it adds Throwing Mastery’s, which a thrown hit doesn’t get. The monster’s defense (a boss’s in Hell at its own level) is first lowered in points by Inner Sight and Attract, then by Conviction, Battle Cry (at most 30%) and Weaken, the three added up; below 0 it adds to your attack rating. Ignore Target’s Defense makes it 0 against a normal monster, a champion or a minion, not against a unique, superunique, boss or player; −% target defense (your gear’s, and your own Blessed Aim’s, its base points) lowers it by that share, half against a superunique, a boss or a player, at most 100%. Chance to hit = 2 × 111 × attack rating / (attack rating + defense) × your level / (your level + its level), at least 5%; above 95% what is left of the 111 counts 90/111, at most 100%, every step rounded down. Smite and Guided Arrow never miss; Bash, Concentrate, Feral Rage and Maul roll as the swing starts, and their hit lands only if that roll did.
  • Crushing blow takes a share of the life the monster has left, whatever its life: 1/8 for a monster (champions and uniques too), 1/30 for a map boss, 1/10 for a player or a pet, and 1/70 for another boss at full life, less as it loses life (1/(70 + 10 for every 1% it is missing)). Each player after the first adds 1.4 to the 8, 30 or 70 (their 70% more life, / 50). A ranged attack divides by 1.5 times as much; crushing blow efficiency multiplies the share by (1 + efficiency / 100). The monster’s physical resistance lowers it (none at 100% or more; pierce doesn’t count). More chance and more efficiency are always better; the kill time shows how much, beside the time without it.
  • Frames per attack come from the IAS Calculator, which has the whole model and plays each attack frame by frame: speed = 100 + the skills’ speed (Fanaticism, Frenzy by its charges, Burst of Speed, Werewolf, the attack’s own) − the weapon’s speed modifier + effective IAS (120 × IAS / (120 + IAS)), 30 less for a sequence, kept between 15 and 175; an animation of N frames takes N × 256 / (its speed × speed / 100) frames, rounded up, minus 1, held. A normal attack is attack 1 or attack 2, half the time each, so it counts both, and it hits with the first weapon only. Two weapons: only the faster one’s speed counts. Zeal, Fend, Fury, Strafe and Dragon Talon rewind their animation between hits (Strafe: its fewest arrows, at one monster); Whirlwind and Blade Dance hit every 6 frames, with each weapon, whatever the attack speed, slows or Frenzy’s charges; Charge’s strike runs at a speed the game sets when it connects, and its damage per second and kill time count the strikes back to back (the run before each strike isn’t counted). A druid’s wereform attacks run at a speed set by the weapon’s attack speed in human form.
  • Next breakpoint: the increased attack speed a build still needs on its other gear (its weapon’s IAS as set) for fewer frames, and what that is worth in damage per second. A build at the most its attack counts shows none.
  • The bosses have their life, defense and physical resistance in Hell: the life of the boss’s own level, +70% for each player after the first (at most 8,388,607). Diablo Clone, Rathma, Mendeln and Lucion have 1.5 times that at tier 0, 4.8 times at tier 1 and 5.6 times at tier 2; their phases, immunity, healing and helpers aren’t counted. The map and dungeon bosses on the game’s map boss lists take crushing blow as map bosses (1/30 of their life); The Tainted Hive, Na-Krul, the two Djinns and Zoltun Kulle aren’t on them and take it as other bosses do. Map modifiers aren’t counted.
  • How they compare: damage per second is the average hit × what critical and deadly strikes add × what the monster’s resistance lets through × hits per second × the chance to hit, so a build’s difference from build A splits exactly into those five. On a build of build A’s class, the fields that differ from build A are marked gold (across classes nearly every field would be).
  • Skills that read another skill’s level: Dragon Claw’s damage counts the level of Claw and Dagger Mastery as its tooltip does; Penetrate’s base points are both Strafe’s synergy and its pierce.
  • Not counted: elemental, poison and magic damage, open wounds, life leech, the monster’s blocking, map modifiers, splash damage to other monsters, mercenaries and summons.

Inspired by HarryPe’s Physical damage calculator.

docs.text:
Season 14 · Attack speed · Breakpoints

Pick your class, attack and weapon and put in your IAS, or start from a common build: the answer box shows your frames and how much more IAS the next breakpoints need.

IAS Calculator Fastest Frames How It’s Worked Out Reference The animation’s numbers Words on this page FramesHow many game frames one attack takes when you hold the button. The game runs 25 frames a second, so fewer is faster. BreakpointThe IAS where the frames drop by one. IAS between two breakpoints changes nothing. IASIncreased attack speed, from your weapon and other gear (and Increased Speed or a corrupted map). It all adds up. EIASEffective IAS: what your IAS is worth after diminishing returns, 120 × IAS ÷ (120 + IAS). WSMA weapon’s speed modifier. Below 0 is faster (a Phase Blade is −30), above 0 slower. Speed100 + skill speed − WSM + EIAS, 30 less for a sequence, kept between 15 and 175. It sets how fast the attack plays. SequenceA skill that plays its own row of animation steps: Jab, Frenzy, Double Swing, Dragon Claw, Blade Fury. CarryThe most IAS a weapon of that base can have (crafted, unique or runeword, Shael in its sockets, the corruption). More, ✓, nowIn the breakpoints: how much IAS you still need for that frame count; ✓ marks the ones you already reach; your row says now.

Fastest held attacks, per class and form

The two fastest frame counts of each class’s normal attack, held, in each form, with every weapon setup that reaches them and the IAS it needs. No skill speed is counted, so Fanaticism, Frenzy, Burst of Speed or the Werewolf skill lower the IAS needed. Click a setup to open it in the calculator.

Attack Weapon type Starts on your setup’s weapon type. Expand all Collapse all What these tables assume How the game turns IAS into frames

Back to the calculator

Worked examples Werewolf and werebear
  • The form takes its speed from your weapon. The game times your class’s own normal attack with the weapon in hand (its frames, and its speed modifier and the IAS on that weapon only, without the diminishing returns), and turns that into the form’s base speed: base = standing frames × 256 ÷ that time. With no weapon the time is 19.
  • Then speed works as in human form: all your IAS, diminished, the weapon’s speed modifier and the skill speed (the Werewolf skill adds its own in werewolf form; Werebear adds none).
  • So IAS on the weapon counts twice, in the form’s base speed and in the speed, and is worth more than IAS on other gear in a form. It keeps counting once speed is at its cap (175), through the base speed, so the calculator’s Breakpoints list IAS on the weapon apart: every frame count from no IAS on the weapon up to the most your weapon can carry.
  • The standing frames are the length of the animation before the attack: a held attack starts from standing (werewolf 9 frames, werebear 10), the first swing out of a run from the run (8).
The rules
  • Numbers are whole numbers. Every division drops the fraction (toward zero), as the game does, but the frame count, which rounds up.
  • Effective IAS: EIAS = 120 × IAS ÷ (120 + IAS). All IAS adds up first: the weapon’s, the rest of your gear’s (arrows and bolts too), a corrupted map’s attack speed for players and Increased Speed’s (which counts as IAS).
  • Speed: 100 + skill speed − WSM + EIAS, 30 less for a sequence skill (Jab, Double Swing, Double Throw, Frenzy, Berserk, Dragon Claw, Blade Fury), then kept between 15 and 175. Skill speed is what auras and skills add: Fanaticism, Frenzy (a fifth of it per charge), Burst of Speed, the Werewolf skill, Double Swing’s +50, Dragon Tail’s −20, Split Throw’s +10.
  • Slows take speed off the same way: being chilled (cold damage) 50 while it lasts, a monster’s Decrepify or Holy Freeze what its skill level gives (a monster’s skills are 3 levels higher in Nightmare and 7 in Hell). Whirlwind’s and Blade Dance’s spin and hits don’t change with slows. They add up, and speed stays at 15 or more.
  • Rate: base speed × speed ÷ 100 per game frame, where one animation frame is 256. Most animations have a base speed of 256; crossbows 294 (Amazon, Assassin, Barbarian) or 282; some Assassin claw attacks 208; sequences 256.
  • Frames per attack, held: ⌈(frames − start) × 256 ÷ rate⌉ − 1. Amazons and Sorceresses start their normal attack a frame in with no weapon and two frames in with a melee weapon or a staff (start 1 or 2), not with a bow, crossbow or claw.
  • Attack 1 or attack 2: the game draws a normal attack (no skill) as attack 1 or attack 2, at random, half the time each. Held, it lasts as long as the one drawn, so the average counts, and the hit comes at attack 1’s hit frame (an attack 2 that ends before it loses its hit). It is always attack 1 with a bow, a crossbow or no weapon and against small monsters (Fallen, Quill Rats, spiders…), always attack 2 against flying ones (birds, bats, wisps…). The two take as long for every class and weapon but an Assassin’s claws (attack 2 is 12 frames to attack 1’s 11) and a Paladin’s two-handed swords (19 to 18): only there does it change your frames.
  • Dual wielding: only one weapon counts, the one with the larger −WSM + its own IAS (on a tie the second weapon): its speed modifier and its IAS. The other weapon’s IAS counts nowhere (in a form the first weapon still sets the base speed). A normal attack hits with the first weapon only. A Barbarian with two weapons swings the dual-wield animations: one-handed swing + swing (1ss), swing + thrust (1js), thrust + thrust (1jt), thrust + swing (1st), by the first weapon’s kind and the second’s. An Assassin with two claws uses the two-claw animations.
  • Two-handed swords use the two-handed animations, except for a Barbarian holding a shield or a second weapon with one.
  • Attacks that repeat in one swing (Zeal, Fury, Fend, Strafe, Dragon Talon): after each hit the animation rolls back by a share (Zeal, Fury and Dragon Talon all the way, Fend 60%, Strafe 50%) and runs to the hit again; the swing lengths are shown hit by hit (4/4/8). Strafe shoots at least as many arrows as its minimum, one per target in range up to its maximum. The game makes the hits on its side: Zeal, Fury and Dragon Talon go all the way back there too, so every hit lands, but for Strafe and Fend it goes back by the frames the swing has taken rather than the animation’s frame, and a hit it hasn’t made when your next attack starts is lost. Held, a Strafe at speed 40 or less shoots only its first arrow (37 or less with a crossbow), Fend at 28 or less hits once (26 or less with a javelin), and with a javelin at speed 172–174 Fend’s third hit comes too late. A hit on the very frame your next attack starts counts as landing, as it does on a steady connection, though a change in ping can make it miss: Strafe’s fifth arrow with a bow at speed 158–175, Fend’s third hit with a javelin at 161–171 or a spear at 175.
  • Whirlwind and Blade Dance hit every 6 frames, their timer, which the game checks every frame: whatever your IAS, slows or Frenzy’s charges, with each weapon when you hold two. The spin turns a step a game frame, whatever the speed.
  • Charge: its run doesn’t depend on IAS. When it connects, the game sets the strike’s speed itself, 100 − WSM + skill speed + EIAS + 65, at most 256, with no base speed: the strike, the last 7 steps of its sequence, lasts ⌈1792 ÷ speed⌉ frames.
  • PD2’s own sequences: Jab is faster than in the original game (one-handed 16 frames, two-handed 18), and so is Blade Fury, a channel: held, the game casts it again every ⌈768 ÷ rate⌉ + 2 frames and throws a blade each time (counted in game: 69 blades in 20 seconds at speed 70, with no weapon and no IAS). Its own timer allows a blade every 4 frames at most, but counted in game it throws one about every 5 frames from speed 100 up, whatever the IAS (95 blades in 20 seconds with Blade Talons and 150 IAS).
  • Cooldowns (Shock Web and Plague Javelin a second, Dragon Flight max(51 − level, 25) frames, Joust max(104 − level × 5 ÷ 2, 38) less what Alma Negra, Leoric’s Mithril Bane or Zerae’s Resolve takes off, at the skill’s level with +skills): the cooldown starts when the skill does what it does (the throw leaves, the strike lands), on the game frame the hit would come, and the game lets the next one start only when it has run out. Held, an attack lasts max(its frames, release + cooldown), standing while it waits: more IAS still helps by bringing the release sooner. Online, the time your connection takes to answer adds to each wait.
  • Mercenaries: 100 − WSM + EIAS + auras, IAS from the weapon and other gear together, no sequence penalty, no start frame. Each shows its own animation whatever it holds. From one attack to the next: ⌈frames × 256 ÷ rate⌉ + 1 frames (+ 2 after a sequence), which the game’s breakpoint screen shows 2 or 3 frames shorter, at the same breakpoints. The Act 5 Barbarian hits twice a swing.
  • Not on this page: casting skills (they follow faster cast rate); Inferno and Arctic Blast (a step a game frame, whatever the speed) and Leap Attack (the other animation rate), which IAS doesn’t change; the mercenaries’ Strafe and Whirlwind; slows from other players (PvP); a map’s attack speed for mercenaries.
A reference implementation

The heart of it in a few lines of JavaScript (the page’s own engine adds the forms, sequences, dual wielding and repeating attacks).

Frames are counted from 1. “Starts 2 in”: an Amazon’s or Sorceress’s normal attack begins 2 frames into its animation, on its 3rd frame.

Weapon damage per second

Average physical damage per second over the merc's Jabs and basic attacks, Critical and Deadly Strikes included, before the target's resistance. Higher is better. Each line is one speed group of elite bases; hover or tap for every group's value, click to set your IAS.

Crushing Blows per second

Every hit rolls Crushing Blow, both hits of a Jab included, so this follows the hit rate alone: the weapon's damage doesn't matter. Infinity's Chain Lightning (25% on striking) fires at the same rate, scaled to 25%.

Seconds to kill the target

Weapon damage (Critical and Deadly Strikes included) and Crushing Blow together, the merc alone. Lower is better. The more each hit does, the more the harder-hitting bases gain on the faster ones, whose edge is the extra Crushing Blows.

Teleporting past a monster

You land on a monster and teleport on one cast later: 8 frames at 105% FCR, 7 frames at 200% FCR. Your merc is moved to where you land in the same frame; if it's free, it acts 2 frames later and Jabs the monster beside it. That Jab plays out in full, both hits on that monster, even after your next teleport has moved the merc on with you: the hit never checks distance. The chart adds up what that one attack does to the monster set above, frame by frame from the frame you land, at your IAS; the markers show when you teleport on.

Base Speed Jab hits on frame Jab length The merc's attack on that monster Landings the merc attacks on, chain teleporting Damage Monster dead 200% FCR (7 frames) 105% FCR (8 frames)

Frames count from the frame you land (frame 0). The attack is one Jab (both hits) or, 20% of the time, one basic attack; damage is its average and "Monster dead" the share of 8,000 simulated attacks per base that kill the monster, with every damage roll, Crushing Blow, Critical Strike and Deadly Strike rolled. A monster killed after you've moved on dies where you left it. While you chain teleport, the merc starts its next attack 2 frames after the last one's length, on whatever is beside it then, so it can attack on only as many landings as its attacks fit: hops of 7 or 8 frames against the length of a Jab (or of a basic attack). Bases of one speed group hit on the same frames; their kill chances differ only through their damage spread.

Every base at 40% IAS Exceptional and normal bases

Ethereal, with your Infinity roll and superior bonus. Ethereal lowers the Strength and Dexterity needed by 10. The best value of each column has a diamond. Within a speed group, average damage differs by about 1% at most, so pick by what your merc can wear. Amazon spears also take Infinity, but the merc can't wear them.

Base Speed Two-hand damage Str / Dex needed Merc level needed Jab length Damage / s Hits / s Crushing Blows / s Kill time

Exceptional and normal bases share the elite bases' speed groups with far less damage: none of them beats the elite base of its speed group.

Jab breakpoints

Item IAS needed for each Jab length, with your skill IAS. A Jab's length covers both of its hits; the merc starts its next attack 2 frames after it; 25 frames make one second.

Basic attack breakpoints

One hit per swing; the merc swings instead of Jabbing 20% of the time.

How it's worked out
  • Attack speed. Item IAS counts as ⌊120 × IAS / (120 + IAS)⌋. Add skill IAS, subtract the base's speed (negative is faster), cap at 75: that's the total. The animation then advances ⌊256 × (100 + total) / 100⌋ per frame. The merc's Jab is a 14-step sequence with two hits (on steps 6 and 10), lasting ⌈256 × 14 / rate⌉ frames; its basic attack is a 16-frame swing with one hit (on frame 11), lasting ⌈256 × 16 / rate⌉ − 1. These give the PD2 wiki's Desert Guard breakpoints exactly. The merc starts its next attack 2 frames after either length: the game ends the attack a frame later, and the merc picks its next one the frame after that. So from one Jab to the next takes the IAS Calculator's frame count for the Desert Mercenary.
  • Attack mix. The merc uses Jab 80% of the time and a basic attack otherwise, so damage and hits per second are averages over that mix (or Jab alone, if you pick it).
  • Damage per hit. First the weapon's own damage: the base's damage, times 1.25 for ethereal, raised by the weapon's enhanced damage, which is Infinity's roll plus a superior base's 5–20% (both are on the weapon, so they add up). That is the damage the weapon shows. A hit does the weapon's damage times (100 + the Strength and Dexterity bonus + Jab's bonus + other damage %) / 100: enhanced damage on the merc's other gear adds to those bonuses, not to the weapon's. Polearms and spears give 0.75% per point of Strength and of Dexterity. Jab gives +30% at level 1 and +15% per level; the merc's Jab is level 24 from merc level 75 on, plus your + skills. A basic attack gets no Jab bonus. A Hell merc has 173 Strength and 139 Dexterity at level 75, then 1.75 and 1.5 more per level.
  • Critical Strike and Deadly Strike. Every hit, both Jab hits included, first rolls Critical Strike (at most 75%): it does 200% damage, plus any Critical Strike Multiplier. A hit that isn't a Critical Strike rolls Deadly Strike (at most 75%, plus any Maximum Deadly Strike): 150% damage, plus any Deadly Strike Multiplier, which adds to the 150% (Wraithskin's +25% makes it 175%). So 50% Deadly Strike alone makes the average hit 25% stronger, and 37.5% with Wraithskin. Only the hit's physical damage is raised; Crushing Blow takes the same share as without. Every base gains the same share, so neither changes which base does the most damage per second.
  • Crushing Blow. Every hit rolls the chance, both Jab hits included. A proc takes the target's current life divided by 8 for most monsters (normal, champion, unique, minion), 30 for map bosses, or 70 + 10 × the % of life it's missing for prime evils. A merc's Crushing Blow works exactly like a player's. Efficiency divides the divisor by (1 + efficiency), a missile multiplies it by 1.5, physical resistance lowers the damage (none at 100%), and with more players in the game the divisor grows (with one player it doesn't).
  • Kill time. Each hit removes the average damage (Critical and Deadly Strikes averaged in) and the average Crushing Blow (chance × share × life left), until no life is left; the hit count divided by hits per second is the time. The merc alone, one player. Baal's life and physical resistance are his Hell values with one player (6,336 base life at 7,792% for his level 99); the map monster and map boss are round examples, so type your own target's.
  • Teleporting. The sorceress's cast is 14 frames at the same speed scale. FCR counts as ⌊120 × FCR / (120 + FCR)⌋, at most 75, and a cast lasts ⌈256 × 14 / rate⌉ − 1 frames: 8 at 105% FCR, 7 at 200%. You land on one cast's teleport frame and leave on the next one's, so you stand on the monster for exactly one cast.
  • The merc during a pass. When you teleport, your merc is moved to where you land in the same frame (except in guild games). If it was free, it acts 2 frames later; if it was in the middle of an attack, that attack keeps going and keeps its target. A Jab's hits land ⌈256 × 5 / rate⌉ and ⌈256 × 9 / rate⌉ frames after it starts, a basic attack's at ⌈256 × 11 / rate⌉, and nothing checks distance between the hit frame and the damage, so a Jab finishes on its first target wherever the merc has been moved. When you walk or run away instead, the merc heads back once you're 19 subtiles away and it has no target (about 34 while it fights), and warps beside you past 48.
  • Not counted. Walking to a target, misses, Chain Lightning's damage, and the merc's own base damage (whether it adds to the weapon's damage isn't confirmed).

docs.title: A run, step by step
docs.text:
1. Open a rare map rolled the way you like it. Rolling for low monster density only buys a safer scout: the events and the boss don't depend on it.
  2. Teleport over the whole map. Map events spawn as the rooms around you fill with monsters, not as monsters die, so a scout finds an event as surely as a full clear does.
  3. Do the event when its message shows, unless you skip it. The Dark Wanderer, the Treasure Fallen and the Corrupted Heroes always bring all three, so stop scouting after the third.
  4. Kill the map boss, which you'll have passed on the scout, and open the next map.
  • When events show: the Spire of Darkness within the first few teleports; the Dark Wanderer, the Treasure Fallen and the Corrupted Heroes from about a quarter of the way in; the Bitter Depths, Horazon, the Shadow of Mendeln, Gheed and the Altar of the Catalyst about halfway through the scout.
  • What decides it: your time a map besides the scout (making the game, opening the map, town) and how long your full clears take. The calculator below shows where the runs pull ahead at your times.
  • Keep Catalyst Shards from the Altar for later maps: each forces an event on one.
  • Unique maps: the bosses of City of Ureh, Warlord of Blood, Na-Krul's Abyss and Djinn's Domain drop extra uniques, or a treasure explosion, every kill. Rush them and leave: Unique maps: rush the bosses.
  • For the grail, put in your missing items under Your grail (it can take your Grail Planner list), and the Corrupted Ear you use: an ear works on every monster of a full clear, but on a run only on the map boss.

docs.title: What stays fixed
docs.text:
• What drops doesn't change with the times, so a time only changes the hours. The drops come from a model of how the game spawns map events and rolls drops: each of the 29 T1-T3 maps played as often, runs on rare maps rolled to low density with no purple line, full clears on rare maps as a clearer keeps them (one corruption), magic find as set plus the map's own.
  • An event rolls on 34% of rare maps, each of the 9 kinds as often. You always find it: the Dark Wanderer, Treasure Fallen and Corrupted Heroes bring all three, and a Bitter Depths map always has its portal. About 1 map in 12 is an event forced by a Catalyst Shard from the Altar.
  • The Bitter Depths: its 20 Lucion chests (3 items from the lesser chest loot and 2 from the better, opened at character level 95 with your magic find and the map's), Zoltun Kulle's own drop and his treasure explosion (60 items of a T3 map boss's loot, with no magic find), and the area's monsters with its 5 elite packs. Its 7 plain chests are left out (about 3% of the event).
  • A skipped event: when it shows (a three-spawn kind at its first spawn, the Spire at its obelisk), you head straight for the boss, since a map has one event and nothing is left to find. You lose its drops and save its time and the rest of the scout. Skipping the Altar also means no Catalyst Shards, so no forced events. Full clears still do every event: a full clear's time includes them.
  • "Worth doing below" compares a run doing the event with one skipping it, by what you compare, with your other times as they are; with your own maps it also counts the maps the event drops (Horazon's six, Treasure Fallen's) and the full clears they save.
  • Teleports per map come from scouting every layout of every map: the fastest route that fills every room an event can spawn in averages 110, a scout that brings every walkable spot on screen 276. A count between them mixes the two; one outside scales the nearer one.
  • A full clear's time includes the event when the map has one, and every full clear kills the boss. Trade value counts each unique and set item at its median asking price on the trade site (softcore ladder, 30 October) and the currency at its median ask (4 November, a stack's price split over its items): runes, Worldstone Shards at 1, Pandemonium keys, Splinters, Corrupted Ears, crafting infusions, essences, scarabs, sigils, unique maps, perfect gems. Catalyst Shards don't count: the model spends each one on a forced event. Asks, not sales.
  • Gold counts Anya's Zakarum and Horadrim Orbs for rolling (2.7 rolls a map for the runs, 1.7 for full clears) and Gheed's offers; the runes, perfect gems and jewels the rolls also eat are left out.

docs.title: How map events spawn
docs.text:
A map rolls its event once, when it is opened: 11% of non-magical, 17% of magic and 34% of rare T1-T3 maps, one of nine kinds at equal odds. Nothing of it exists until it spawns. A room fills with monsters the first time you come near it: standing in one room fills it and the 8 rooms around it, about 24 tiles across, and a teleport fills the block around where you land. Each newly filled room may bring the event, more likely the more of the map's rooms are filled already; the event then stands in that room or one beside it, and its message shows.

Once you use its obelisk, half the new rooms bring a group of shadows, until 6 keys or nine tenths of the rooms1

How many rooms count as the whole map is set per map, from the Lost Temple's few to the Halls of Torture's many, and the empty blocks at a map's edges count too. A spawn needs open ground near the room's centre, about 2.4 tiles across, so the crowded corners of a map take none. Scouting every room is what makes the late kinds show: a scout that skips parts of the map can miss them.

Season 14 · Maps · Erazure's loot filter

The filter puts two experience lines on identified maps, under their other highlights. The first, on uncorrupted maps, says how good the map's rolls are: whether it's worth corrupting. The second, on every map, says what the map is worth to your character right now. This page explains both, and shows how your level and a map's size change the second one.

11.48x Experience 21.14x at Level 89 Experience: +15% Monster Density: +47% 11.48x Experience

How much the map's rolls add to it. The same for every character. On uncorrupted maps only.

21.14x at Level 89

What the map is worth to you: experience for the distance you walk, against an average plain map, at your level.

Rule of thumb: pick which map to run by the "at Level" line. The "Experience" line tells you whether an uncorrupted map rolled well enough to corrupt.

1.48x Experience: how good the rolls are

A full clear of this map with its rolls, against the same map with no rolls: 1.48x means the rolls add 48%. Which map it is doesn't matter here, only what its rolls add to it, and your level doesn't change it.

  • What counts: Monster Density (more monsters), Monster Rarity (more champion and unique packs), Experience, Area Level (higher level monsters, each worth more), Fortified (half as many monsters, each worth double) and "Map contains ..." monsters (one more kind of monster in the mix).
  • What doesn't: anything that makes monsters easier or harder to kill, and the loot rolls.
  • Where it shows: uncorrupted T1–T3 maps and T4 dungeons. It's there to tell you whether a map is worth corrupting; once it's corrupted, its rolls are settled and the "at Level" line says what it's worth to you. Unique maps don't show it: their rolls never change.
Its color

The color of the tag's number says how the rolls compare with other maps of the same tier (the word Experience is always gold). Every tier is cut about the same way among uncorrupted rare maps: about 1 in 6 shows no line, about half are gold, 1 in 4 red and 1 in 12 purple (a little fewer red and purple in T1, more in T3). Most magic maps, about 4 in 5, show no line. T4 dungeons always show it: about 6 in 10 gold, 3 in 10 red and 1 in 10 purple. Can't tell the colors apart? The tag's number decides its color: compare it with this table.

Tier No line Gold Red Purple

T4 dungeons are cut among their uncorrupted rare dungeons, which come from the Horadric Cube (a T3 map and a Dungeon Scarab) with +40–50% experience besides their rolls.

1.2x at Level 89: what the map is worth to you This map with its rolls: the experience of a full clear, for you, divided by the distance you walk to clear it The average non-magical T1–T3 map: the same, for you

1.0x is an average plain map. 1.1x is 10% more experience for the same distance walked. Below 1.0x, an average plain map would do better. T4 dungeons are compared with the average plain T3 map instead.

  • The map itself: how many monsters spawn, how many champion and unique packs, their level, and the bosses in its layout.
  • Its rolls: the same ones as in the Experience line.
  • The distance: every map has a clear path, the route that takes you close to 95% of the places its monsters spawn (most players clear 90–95% of a map), starting where you arrive and averaged over its layouts. A big, spread-out map takes longer to clear, so its experience counts for less.
  • Your level: monsters well below your level give less experience. More on that below.
  • Your own +% experience: the map's Experience roll adds to the bonus you already have; it doesn't multiply it. So it's worth less the more you have: with +50% of your own, a map's +15% gives you 10% more, not 15%.
Its color

The color of the line's number says how far ahead of an average plain map this map is for you (the words "at Level" are always gold). On T1–T3 and unique maps the number alone decides it, so a 2.5x is purple at any level. T4 dungeons, compared with the T3 maps and far ahead of them, have cuts of their own, which rise from level 95. Can't tell the colors apart? Compare the number with this table.

Maps Gold Red Purple

Of rare T1–T3 maps, about 1 in 3 shows red or purple and 1 in 20 purple. Corrupted T2 and T3 maps, the ones most players run at high levels, are red or purple far more often: about two in three at level 94. Dungeons are made from T3 maps and can be corrupted like them, so their cuts give them about as much color as a T3 map at your level: an uncorrupted dungeon as often as an uncorrupted T3 map, a corrupted one as often as a corrupted T3 map (at level 94, about 1 in 4 uncorrupted rare dungeons shows red or purple, and two in three corrupted ones, 1 in 5 of them purple). A dungeon's line climbs from level 95, because the T3 maps it's compared with give you less experience from there while the dungeon's own monsters don't yet, and its cuts climb with it.

At your level

Set your level in the bar at the top of the page: this section and the example's table follow it.

Experience from each monster at level 89

Map monsters are level 87 in T1, 88 in T2, 89 in T3 and 92 in T4 dungeons. Champions are 2 levels higher, uniques and their minions 3. A monster up to 5 levels below you gives full experience, and each level more takes 19% off, down to 5%. A monster above your level gives your level divided by its level.

Tier Normal monsters Champions+2 levels Uniques and minions+3 levels The average plain map of each tier

Your level counts for the average map too, so it only moves the line where a map's monsters are lower or higher than average. Up to about level 92 hardly anything moves. From there, T1 maps fall behind and T3 maps pull ahead, and an Area Level roll is worth more.

    2. The map: a plain Sanatorium has about as many monsters as the average map (its full clear: 1.01x), but its clear path is 1.32x the average's, one of the longest of the T1 maps. Per distance walked that's 0.77x.

    Your level This map With +50% of your own With +1 Area Level What it leaves out
    • How fast you kill: monster life, damage, resistances and immunities, and your build. It assumes the time a clear takes grows with the distance you walk.
    • Loot: Magic Find and the drop rolls.
    • Random map events.
    • Everything between maps: time in town, loading screens, opening maps.
    Good to know
    • The lines show on identified maps only: an unidentified map has no rolls yet. The "Experience" line shows on uncorrupted T1–T3 maps and T4 dungeons only.
    • The "at Level" line shows for characters of level 80–98. At level 99 there's no experience to gain, so there's no line.
    • The tag is cut to two decimals, so its number always matches its color: 1.649 shows as 1.64x. The "at Level" line is rounded to two decimals: 1.155 shows as 1.16x, and 0.999 as 1.00x. Its color follows the number shown, so 1.996 is a red 2.00x.
    • They are estimates, worked out from how maps are built and how monsters spawn, not counted in game.
    How it's worked out
    • Monsters. Every area of a map spawns monsters in its rooms. Monster Density adds spawns, up to a limit each area has. Champion and unique packs fall between the area's own minimum and maximum, and Monster Rarity raises both. Fortified halves the spawns and doubles each monster's experience. A "Map contains ..." monster joins the area's own monsters as one more kind, picked for about 1 spawn in 10 (1 in 7 to 1 in 20, depending on the area). The bosses and monsters placed in a map's layout count too.
    • Experience per monster. It follows the monster's level: the map's area level, plus any Area Level roll (each level is worth about 2.5% more around level 87), 2 more for champions and 3 more for uniques and their minions.
    • Your level. Each kind of monster gets the level penalty above: 81%, 62%, 43%, 24% and then 5% for a monster 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 or more levels below you. Then your own +% experience and the map's are added together and applied.
    • Clear path. Measured on the map's own layouts, starting where you arrive (the map start on the wiki's layout pictures: on T1–T3 maps, the waypoint): walk to the nearest place a monster can spawn that you haven't come within 7 tiles of yet, then put those stops in the shortest order found and walk them again, leaving out the hardest-to-reach places, until you've come within 7 tiles of 95% of them. Averaged over every layout of the map, and over walks begun at the start and a few steps from it. Horazon's Memory's lightning spires are left out (players walk past them).
    • The 1.0x. The average of the 29 T1–T3 maps with no rolls: their average experience for you over their average clear path. For T4 dungeons, the average of the T3 maps.

• +% damage adds up, then multiplies the physical part once. One pool holds the map's Enhanced Physical Damage, Fortified's 40, the elite bonus (Hell: champion 66, Berserker 198), Extra Strong (unique 99, its minions 49) and Might, Concentration or Fanaticism.
  • Deadly strike multiplies the physical part by 1.5, after that pool. It never touches elemental damage.
  • Many monsters' attacks carry elemental damage of their own, on every hit or on a share of them, which grows with the monster's level and the players in the game as its physical damage does. Spectral Hit's element takes the place of the attack's own damage of that element.
  • Elemental damage of one kind is one roll. "Physical damage as extra", the attack's own, Fire, Cold and Lightning Enchanted, Holy Fire and Holy Shock's added damage and Spectral Hit all add to it; then the skill damage mods (Flaming, Hibernal, Static, Toxic and Fortified's) raise it. +% damage and deadly strike don't.
  • "Physical damage as extra" is a share of the monster's base attack, before the +% pool and deadly strike. The poison version's number is per frame: over its 5 seconds it deals 125/256 of what it says (163% shown is about 80%).
  • Enchanted uniques add 66–100% of their level's damage figure to their attacks in that element; their minions 33–50%.
  • Spectral Hit adds 66–100% of the unique's level damage figure to each attack in one random element: fire, lightning, magic, cold or poison (1 attack in 5 each). Its poison is a per-frame figure too: alone it deals 40/256 of it over 1.6 seconds. On a map that adds poison, a hit with both lasts 290 frames instead of 125, so all of its poison deals 290/256 of its figure.
  • Aura Enchanted gives a unique one of eight monster auras (Conviction, Fanaticism, Holy Shock, Holy Freeze, Holy Fire, Might, Concentration, Vigor) at its level / 7, at most 13: a unique is 3 levels above the area, so that's level 12 in T1 maps and 13 in T2 and up (or with +1 area level). Holy Fire, Holy Freeze and Holy Shock add their damage to the unique's own attacks; Vigor changes no hit numbers here.
  • Cursed casts Amplify Damage on 3 of a unique's hits in 4, at its level / 5 + 1: level 19 in T1–T3 maps, 20 in T4 dungeons.
  • Some bosses have an aura of their own, always on, and its damage joins their attacks: Son of Rakkis's Holy Shock (level 15) and Shattered Soul's Holy Freeze (level 10).
  • The 5% double comes last and doubles everything in the hit. With deadly strike too, the physical part is 3x. It's each monster's own chance (5% for nearly all; T4 dungeons' Blood Bringers, the Outer Void's Void Knights and the bosses Gregus Mazi, Overlord Aerlynn and Warlord of Blood have none), and it doubles spells and missiles as well as melee hits.
  • A boss's spells deal their own damage, at their skill level (7 higher in Hell than in Normal): the monster's level and the players in the game don't change it. The map's +% fire, cold, lightning and poison skill damage and Fortified's raise its elemental part, as they do the attack's; a few missiles carry damage of their own that they don't raise. The +% damage pool, deadly strike, "physical damage as extra" and the attack's own elemental damage only reach the spells that strike with a share of the boss's attack (that share of each).
  • Fire on the ground (a fire wall, the burning ground a meteor or a blaze leaves) hits again and again while you stand in it, up to 25 times a second, and takes its share of your flat damage reduction each time: the page shows a second standing in it.
  • Fortified adds 40 to the +% damage pool, though the orb's text says +20%.
  • Curses and Conviction lower your totals, the same way the map's -resist does. Your physical damage reduction counts up to 50% against a hit and your resistances up to your maximum (at most 90%), so anything above that soaks them first. Amplify Damage and Decrepify lower physical damage reduction; Lower Resist lowers fire, cold, lightning and poison; Conviction fire, cold and lightning.
  • Crushing blow ignores the hit's damage: it takes a tenth of your current life, less your whole physical damage reduction (curses included, not capped at 50%). At 100% or more it does nothing.
  • Flat damage reduction comes off physical damage before the percentage; magic damage reduction off fire, cold, lightning and magic. Poison ignores both.
  • Each player after the first adds 6.25% to monsters' base attack damage (and 70% to their life).
  • Not counted here: how often you're hit (attack rating, defense, block, attack speed), the pulse damage of the auras a monster gets from a unique mod or a monster near it (Holy Fire, Holy Shock, Holy Freeze), open wounds, absorb, poison length reduction, how many of a spell's bolts or shards reach you, and the spells and missiles of monsters other than bosses.
